cross_area_duplicates.why: Engine & technical, Features, Plan, scope & sequencing and Market & competition all recommended shipping the package early as a probe, option a here. Engine & technical would first fix the left-edge list bug and the spaced-key bug; Market & competition would make the release the launch. Licence and package shape are decided separately.

Features and Product & definition recommended the same as option a here: run the five-regex comparison before any tier is priced on the certificate. Market & competition recommended a different first step: fix the CLI, run the certificate end to end once, then decide. Which tiers exist at all is decided in Pricing & tiers.

Features recommended keeping retention and specifying it as an append-only file inside the review store, which is option a here. Plan, scope & sequencing recommended option d: publish no Pro price until the team conversations say what teams are gated on. Neither recommended gating Pro on attribution.

Business & operations and Product & definition both recommended deleting the document-holding design, option b here. Business & operations would decide publishing separately, after the sharing decision; Product & definition would also delete the public route. Its idea of a permalink that renders a public GitHub URL is an option on the Features share-page card.

Go-to-market & channels recommended keeping the page live, rendered from the repo with no stored snapshot and noindex by default, closest to option b here. Market & competition recommended option d, permalink plus export. If the page survives, who may publish and whether it is indexed is a separate Legal, privacy & data decision.

Business & operations recommended much the same as option d here: commit to a weekly density, count achieved days every Friday, re-cut at week 4. Product & definition recommended cutting scope instead, which is option c: fix-first plus review state in the pilot, six features moved to the build after it.

Market & competition asked the same question with near-identical options and recommended the same answer, option c here: one core, extension first, standalone second. Its only different option was to defer until the raw-write data-loss path is tested.

Access, offline & install asked which build the ten pilot users get and recommended the same as option b here: the web app against a GitHub repo. Its remaining option, adding the file-access days and restating the schedule, belongs with the schedule decision in Plan, scope & sequencing.

Business & operations recommended owning the fork outright, option c here: absorb the shell and keep sgnk-md parked. Plan, scope & sequencing recommended pinning the shell as a versioned internal package, closest to freezing it, option b. Whether the product is still called a markdown editor is a separate Product & definition question.

Flow & interaction and Design, UI & attention both recommended the typed refusal return, option b here. Two narrower questions stay open under it: where a refusal is placed, which Flow & interaction answered with its placement ladder, and how it is shown, which Design, UI & attention answered with a line under the field.

Research & evidence asked only when to run the test, and recommended running it in week 0 and making it the demo. That matches option a here: prove the anchor survives a real agent rewrite before committing the eighteen days.

Business & operations and Market & competition both recommended asking both maintainers in week 0, in writing, before the channel depends on them; Market & competition would publish whatever they answer. No option here asks both first: option a opens a PR to both after the MCP server is built, option b asks superpowers only.

Market & competition recommended publishing no price until the twenty team conversations return, close to option d here. Business & operations recommended taking a single $30 per editor per month into them and negotiating down, above any number here. Whether cross-person review state is the paid gate is the Pro gate card in this area.

Market & competition and Product & definition both recommended option b here: coarse authorship free, span-level authorship paid. Market & competition drew the free line at commit granularity rather than file level. Making attribution the headline is also an option on the Product & definition card about the headline.

Legal, privacy & data and Research & evidence both recommended paying an attorney for a knock-out search on two names now, option a here, rather than reading the registers ourselves first. The legal card's rename options are covered by the name decision in this area.

Market & competition asked the same question and recommended the same answer, option c here: take a clean coined name. Its fourth option, approaching the incumbent's author first, is a separate card in this area.

Plan, scope & sequencing recommended verifying export and going client-side if only the server half fails, close to option b here. Product & definition asked only whether export stays in the pilot: verify it, and remove the menu if it fails. Deleting the server PDF route is also asked in Access, offline & install.

Product & definition recommended the same as option b here: ship both and attach the founder test notes this week. Plan, scope & sequencing recommended cutting both, option d, along with the file-scoped AI, keeping only the scan with no model. Its option to settle the form factor first is carried by the form-factor card.

Legal, privacy & data asked whether to rewrite the web app to a browser-only path before the first stranger or withdraw the zero-bytes claim, and recommended the rewrite. Option b here is that rewrite (option a would be too); option c is withdrawing the claim.

Market & competition asked the same question with near-identical options and recommended the same answer, option b here: narrow the headline to per-span review state kept in the repo. Its only different option was to decide nothing until the weeks 1-2 tests run.

Flow & interaction recommended one review file per person, option c here. This card recommends the opposite shape: one shared file, merged as a union and deduplicated on read. Flow & interaction's question also covered what a teammate sees.
Design, UI & attention asked the same question with the same four choices and recommended the same answer, option a here: surface only what a stated rule selects, and keep the rest one step away.

Flow & interaction asked the same question and recommended the same answer, option b here: keep the colour and add one non-colour mark. It specified the mark as a one-pixel left rule on the span, with no icon.

Features asked the same question and recommended the same answer, option b here: budget the cheap half of the editing floor. Its cheap half names rebinding Cmd-K to insert-link, which this option does not list.

Access, offline & install also recommended a client-side index, but built lazily as files are opened, which is option a here, not the whole-repo worker index. Where the browser gets the bytes from is decided on that area's web byte-path card.

Research & evidence asked whether the two-week tests ask about money, and recommended the same as option a here: a price question with both price rungs in the script. It would ask it in all forty conversations, not only the twenty with teams. It sets no kill threshold.

Research & evidence recommended recruiting from the founders' client list, plus sgnk-md's users if that list exists, which is the warm-network route of option b here. Contacting sgnk-md's users as one source is a separate card in this area.
Plan, scope & sequencing asked the same question and recommended the same answer, option a here: record a one-person build and re-derive every estimate, date and cap at a one-person rate.

Legal, privacy & data asked only which instrument ships and recommended the local file as drafted, pasted once by each person, option a here; it did not take up interviewing everyone. Its rotating install id stays a named non-option. Where the file can live is an Access, offline & install card.

Research & evidence recommended the same as option d here: settle whether we hold user documents and make the repo say one thing, then buy the review. Its question also asked whether the review comes before the pilot or before the first team customer.

Market & competition recommended the same as option b here: keep the position and write the rebuttal naming Zed. It also adds Delta to the market table. It did not separate the review file from prose.

Product & definition asked about Almanac and Zed Delta together and recommended naming both first, unprompted, with dates and stated causes. For Almanac that is option a here. How Delta is answered is on the Engine & technical card about the CRDT rebuttal.

Go-to-market & channels asked whether to call it a markdown editor in public, and recommended a split no option here offers: keep 'markdown editor' as the internal definition, never in public copy. Its option to rename the category matches option b here.

Go-to-market & channels asked which refusals may be stated in public and recommended publishing only the three that are true and differentiating today, closest to option c here. This card recommends one reconciled list with a reversal price on each entry.

Market & competition recommended allowing out-of-process extension only, and saying so explicitly, which is the out-of-process half of option b here. This card recommends keeping the ban and no longer calling community the first moat.

Market & competition recommended moving the merge, but not the transport, into the build after the pilot. That is the same choice as option c here: the user's git carries the files and we handle the conflicts. It adds a timing, the build after the pilot, which this option leaves open.

Product & definition recommended the opposite order, option b here: ship broken links and missing standard docs, and defer staleness. Its question also asked whether the scan is a product feature or the consultancy's diagnostic; selling services off the scan is a Go-to-market & channels card.

Features recommended a cheaper route no option here names: make the web app responsive enough to read and mark reviewed on a phone, rather than a separate mobile reviewer with its own budget and date.

Go-to-market & channels also recommended building it early, but as the demo surface for the three landing pages, not as a channel. On shipping it, that is option a here; whether it is ever counted as a channel follows from this card.

Go-to-market & channels recommended renaming the whole product first and then shipping the extension under the new name, option a here, not shipping it as mdmax. The naming itself is decided in Name & identity.

Plan, scope & sequencing asked the same question and recommended the same answer, option a here: no Obsidian surface, and delete every remaining mention. It adds rewriting the plan's no-go branch as services and engine. A Market & competition card that pairs an Obsidian extension with the ?src= link is separate.
Product & definition asked the same question and recommended the same answer, option a here: keep answer-in-place in the pilot as specified, markers only, two days.

Access, offline & install asked the narrower question of the app identifier and recommended the same as option b here: a vendor-scoped identifier now, with the display name free to change. What that means for signing and updates is on the Access, offline & install signing card.

link_edges.why: An extension inherits about 6.5 of 17.5 table-stakes days from the host; a standalone shell pays them. The surface decides the day count the schedule publishes.
An extension inherits the host's interaction floor and keymap, so the floor budget is only spent if the standalone shell wins.
The name collides only in the VS Code store. No extension, no collision, and the bare word becomes survivable.
Two of the savings that make the extension attractive are proven on VS Code and nowhere else; the fork test changes which surface option is right.
Six of the generation block's days disappear if the surface is VS Code, which changes whether F5/F6 are worth keeping in MVP-0.
How many surfaces one person can carry at 1.21 engineering days a week is a different number if a second founder is signed.
Offline reading is only a question on the web surface. Desktop-first makes AC12 moot.
Bundling the frontend, scoping the fs capability and setting a CSP are only worth doing if a desktop build ships at all.
On the web every review action is a repository write; on desktop it is a local file write. The write-back shape follows the surface.
Which surface the pilot runs on decides where a later out-of-band write is noticed, and therefore what the cold-start baseline can be.
Cutting Live mode from MVP-0 settles the editor-mode count; keeping it makes four modes the default.
The Obsidian surface and Live-mode rendering fidelity are the two halves of one bet; killing the plugin removes the reason to chase fidelity.
Shipping the engine as a free package is exactly the thing whose licence, package split and name E24 decides.
The one-week package probe and hand recruitment compete for the same founder launch hours in the same quarter.
The MCP write path is where a repo-level agent write-scope control would live; no MCP server, no place to put it.
If the MCP server is the sanctioned third-party surface, the plugin ban's exception and the package probe are the same commitment.
The chosen byte path either forbids or permits a server-side search index, which is F25's whole question.
The server PDF route is two of export's five menu items; deleting it changes which export option is right.
Where the user's AI key can live on the web determines whether a bring-your-own-key gate is even buildable before the pilot.
Three of the four access paths cannot hold the usage file as designed, so the instrument choice is constrained by where it can physically sit.
If we hold zero document bytes the hosted share route cannot stay as built; if we adopt the Firestore design it can.
The sign-in gate exists because of the Firebase design. Delete the design and the login screen loses its reason to be first.
The projection law's store cap is a function of whether a control-plane document store exists at all.
A frontmatter mark on published pages presupposes published pages that are open to somebody; founder-only publishing removes the channel.
Who answers the six-hour CERT-In clock is one of the three items B14 sequences; B14 cannot be scheduled without L4's answer.
GST registration status decides whether we can bill direct or need a merchant of record from the first sale.
Whether the sidecar carries a real identity or a pseudonymous id changes what each JSONL line holds and therefore how it merges.
Retention floors set by law and the paid retention window are the same journal; a deletion promise constrains where it may live.
The repository currently has no licence at all, so the engine's publication licence and the repo's licence must be decided in one pass.
If attribution leads, F3 stops being a free hover card and becomes the product; if review state leads, F3's split-paid option is the live one.
The weeks 1-2 test arms are the candidate headlines; settling the headline changes how many arms are worth running.
Naming Almanac first is only forced if review state stays the pitch; a narrowed or authorship-led headline changes the disclosure.
Byte-exactness cannot go into public copy while the trailing-comment deletion refutes it; the fix's timing decides the claim's.
The repo-report cold-open demo is the docs scan; which half of F7 ships decides whether that demo exists.
The projection law says every view owns no state, and review state is a store beside the file. F1's store design is what the law is being amended for.
Whether relocation survives an out-of-band write depends entirely on what the anchor record carries; E22 chooses the pointer F1 is testing.
Shared review state is the candidate reason seats exist, so proving or narrowing the anchor changes what Pro can gate on.
The hover card's rows and their sources are determined by whether attribution is free, split, or the headline.
The engagement is sold off the docs scan; whether the scan ships, and which half, decides whether it can be sold before it runs.
A bring-your-own-key hard gate cuts the processor chain to nothing; operator keys keep five foreign providers to paper.
Reframing sync as conflict surfacing over the user's git is only coherent under the never-a-CRDT position; reopening it changes the sync shape.
The 83% folder-scan refusal is literally what a stranger meets in the first thirty seconds; NF-1's fix decides whether first run is gateable.
A third 'seen' state adds an action-kind field to every sidecar line, which changes the merge and dedupe rules.
How many surfaces carry an unreviewed count only makes sense once you know whether the primary surface enumerates or suppresses.
Whether the five-second tint test is a build-stopping gate sets its sample size and pass line; the two cards currently imply n=10 and n=15.
Single-letter review keys and Tab-to-indent are one keymap with one WCAG 2.1.4 duty; they cannot be decided apart.
The blocking contrast gate is a CI job, and there is no CI. D12's option (a) is unbuildable until E12 lands.
Selling review gates that block in CI presumes we run CI ourselves and know what it costs to keep green.
Whether Max survives as a third rung depends on whether the certificate is a product or a 200-line linter.
The public web checker with the dataset and the public frontmatter validator are the same page and the same founder hours.
Publishing any engine number as one fraction requires the second, agent-written population that R7 decides whether to pin.
Non-Latin correctness is one scope line: the engine's key predicate and offset fix, and the interface's stated CJK/RTL support, must agree.
The shelf the buyer files this under sets the price on that shelf; on the markdown-editor shelf the price is zero.
A few-hundred-customer business and a $4-5 seat price do not both survive; accepting the small shape forces the higher rung or services.
The price question and its kill number are asked of the cohorts G15 recruits; a warm studio list and a cold code-search list give different evidence.
The fortnight's test schedule is where the price question and any pre-order arm actually run; sequencing decides whether both fit.
Every density, date and break-even in the schedule is denominated in founders; the count changes the published number by 41 to 70 per cent.
What 'the pilot passed' means is unobservable unless the instrument that observes it is chosen first.
The support coefficient is the largest cost in the free tier; measuring it or not decides whether free can stay uncapped.
Which buyer the first version serves decides which gate Pro can plausibly charge for and whether F5/F6 stay in MVP-0.

notes:
Read all 261 cards across 15 files (AC 15, B 15, D 19, E 28, F 26, FL 14, FF 11, G 21, L 19, MK 24, N 8, PL 14, PR 16, P 18, R 13).

SCALE OF THE DUPLICATION. 43 duplicate sets covering 103 cards; 60 cards fall away, leaving 201. Market & competition loses 12 of 24 and Plan, scope & sequencing loses 8 of 14 — both areas were largely re-asking decisions owned elsewhere. Engine & technical loses only 1 of 28 and Legal 4 of 19, which is what you would expect from areas that own mechanisms rather than commentary.

THE TWO WORST. (1) The free-engine package probe is asked five times (FF12/E31/F14/PL14/MK11) with five different recommendations — run it first, run it after the engine fixes, run both, ship MIT this month, make it the launch. (2) The rendering certificate's bake-off is asked four times (E6/F30/MK22/P21). A meeting working from the un-merged set would answer each independently and ship a contradiction.

RECOMMENDATION CONFLICTS INSIDE DUPLICATE SETS. About twenty sets carry disagreeing recs. The sharpest: what Pro gates on (PR1 attribution / F12 retention-as-sidecar / PL15 don't price yet); the hosted share route (F19 disable / G10 keep with noindex / MK18 permalink plus export); the ?src= parameter (FF7 ship in MVP-0 / G25 demo only); the sidecar layout (E37 shared file with merge=union / FL16 one file per person — both rec "a", for opposite shapes); the extension name (FF5 ship as mdmax / G21 rename the product first); the security review (L16 shrink the product first / R12 review firestore.rules now). Merging is not cosmetic here: it forces a single answer where three exist.

CARDS I DELIBERATELY DID NOT MERGE. L6 (publishing governance) is not F19 — it decides noindex and system slugs once the route survives. MK7 is not G2 — it bundles the ?src= replacement. F10 is not L10 — L10's DPA and sub-processor options have no counterpart in F10. AC14 is not F16 — F16 also decides folder-to-one-PDF. E18 is not R7, D22 is not E33, D18 is not FL11: each pair shares one axis but carries a genuinely different option set, so they are edges instead.

LINK EDGES. Capped at 60 and biased to cross-area, since intra-area dependency is already carried by each card's own "linked" array. Absence from this list is therefore NOT evidence a card is isolated — I dropped roughly forty real edges to fit the cap, including B14 to L7/L19, G6 to G8, N1 to N2, F5 to F10, L21 to R18, F16 to G12, E18 to G9, MK31 to L23, R11 to D20, FF4 to R7, G4 to PL17, and most of the Engine-internal chain (E1/E15/E16/E17/E20/E21/E23/E26 to E12).

ORPHANS. Seven cards change nothing else's right answer and nothing changes theirs. D13 (Google CDN icon font) and PR19 (grandfathering) are real but self-contained hygiene. L22 (children/age gate) and MK21 (the Djot arithmetic) are one-line written positions. MK17 (competitive re-read cadence) is process with no downstream. R5 (evidence tags) and R6 (withdrawals ledger gating the PDF build) are document hygiene for the plan itself rather than product decisions — worth asking whether they belong in this set at all, or in a separate editorial checklist.

ONE STRUCTURAL OBSERVATION. Four areas — Market & competition, Plan, scope & sequencing, Product & definition and Research & evidence — write mostly ABOUT decisions owned in Engine, Features, Form factor, Pricing and Legal. After the merge they hold the genuinely distinctive cards (MK13 incumbent response, MK16 market size, MK29 the graveyard, PL3 fix-first order, PL5 the exit bar, PL10 kill conditions, P11 the demo, P13 the projection law, P24 what review claims, R1 stop-the-rounds, R7 the second corpus, R18 verbatim-only). If a further pass is wanted, those four are where to look for a second round of re-framing rather than duplication.
